Iceland (Icelandic: Island) had a population of 389,444 on 1 January 2025.[1][2] The total fertility rate was 1.56 children per woman in 2023,[3] down from 2.2 in 2009. Life expectancy at birth is 82.6 years (80.9 for men, 84.3 for women).[4] About 18.2% of residents are immigrants; the largest groups are Poles (23,000), Lithuanians (5,800) and Romanians (4,000). The Reykjavik capital region (Hofudborgarsvaedid) holds 244,177 people, or 63% of the total. Net migration in 2023 was +6,790; births 4,315; deaths 2,571.

search.text: The current population of Iceland is 402,329 as of 2026, based on the latest United Nations data.\n
As of 1 January 2025 the population of Iceland was 389,444. About 63% live in the Capital Region.\n
The population of Iceland was 391,810 at the end of the fourth quarter of 2025, 201,160 males and 190,460 females.\n
Iceland has a population of 401,014 in 2026, growing 0.71% per year, ranked 180th in the world.\n
Iceland is a Nordic island country between the North Atlantic and Arctic Oceans. Population estimate 2025: 389,444.\n

page.text: The current population of Iceland is 402,329 as of Friday, October 9, 2026, based on Worldometer's elaboration of the latest United Nations data.\n
Iceland 2025 population is estimated at 398,266 people at mid-year.\n
Iceland population is equivalent to 0.0048% of the total world population.\n
Iceland ranks number 180 in the list of countries (and dependencies) by population.\n
The population density in Iceland is 4 per Km2 (10 people per mi2).\n
The total land area is 100,250 Km2 (38,707 sq. miles).\n
93.5 % of the population is urban (372,460 people in 2025).\n
The median age in Iceland is 36.9 years.\n

Iceland is a Nordic island country between the North Atlantic and Arctic Oceans, on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge between North America and Europe. It is the most sparsely populated country in Europe. Its capital and largest city is Reykjavik, and the surrounding Capital Region is home to roughly two thirds of the residents of the country.\n

The population has grown in most years since records began. Growth in the last decade came mostly from immigration: workers in tourism, construction and fishing, many of them from Poland and Lithuania, and their families. Births still exceed deaths, although the fertility rate has fallen below the level needed to keep the population stable without migration.\n

Year: as of July 1 of the year indicated.\n

Population: overall total population (both sexes and all ages) in the country as of July 1 of the year indicated, as estimated by the United Nations, Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division. For forecasted years, the medium fertility variant is used.\n

Yearly % Change: for the latest year, the percentage change in total population over the last year. For all other years, the latest year annual percentage change equivalent assuming homogeneous change in the preceding five year period, calculated through reverse compounding.\n

Yearly Change: for the latest year, the absolute change in total population (increase or decrease in number of people) over the last year. For all other years, the average annual numerical change over the preceding five year period.\n

Migrants (net): the average annual number of immigrants minus the number of emigrants over the preceding five year period, or subsequent five year period for the latest data. A negative number means that there are more emigrants than immigrants.\n

Median Age: the age that divides the population into two numerically equal groups: half of the people are older than the median age indicated and half are younger. This parameter provides an indication of age distribution.\n

Fertility Rate: the average number of children an average woman will have during her reproductive period, expressed as children per woman. A value of about two is needed to keep the population stable where there is no migration.\n
